title: HIVE Doctor — Micro-anatomy: the body sliced to the cell
author: Jeff
safety: Educational micro-anatomy/histology reference. Not a diagnosis. Pending clinician sign-off.

entries.scale: whole body → organ → tissue → CELL → organelle

layers.detail: A thin oily barrier controlling what enters and leaves the cell.
The jelly interior where reactions happen and organelles sit.
The control centre holding DNA (the genetic instructions).
The 'power plants' that make energy (ATP) — plentiful in busy cells like heart and muscle.
Build and fold proteins.
Packages and ships proteins.
Recycling and clean-up units.

entries.function: The cell is the smallest living unit; trillions of specialised cells build every tissue and organ.
entries.clinical: Many diseases start at the cell: too little energy (mitochondrial problems), uncontrolled division (cancer), or cell death from lost blood supply (a heart attack is heart-muscle cells dying).
entries.source: HIVE Doctor original micro-anatomy reference (standard public-domain histology, re-expressed)

entries.scale: organ surface → epithelial sheet → epithelial cells

layers.detail: Covers surfaces and lines cavities, glands, and vessels — a barrier and a gateway.
Squamous (flat — for exchange, e.g. air sacs), cuboidal, columnar (tall — lining the gut), and glandular (secreting).
Tightly joined cells sitting on a basement membrane; they renew quickly.

entries.function: Protection, absorption, secretion, and filtration happen at epithelial surfaces.
entries.clinical: Most cancers (carcinomas) arise from epithelium. Barrier breakdown lets in infection.
entries.source: HIVE Doctor original micro-anatomy reference (standard public-domain histology, re-expressed)

entries.scale: body framework → connective tissue → fibres + cells + matrix

layers.detail: Supports, binds, and protects — the body's scaffolding and packing.
Loose/fatty tissue, dense fibrous (tendons, ligaments), cartilage, bone, and blood (a fluid connective tissue).
Cells scattered in a matrix of fibres (collagen, elastin) and ground substance.

entries.function: Holds the body together, cushions, stores energy (fat), and (as blood) transports.
entries.clinical: Collagen disorders weaken joints and vessels; cartilage wear causes osteoarthritis.
entries.source: HIVE Doctor original micro-anatomy reference (standard public-domain histology, re-expressed)

entries.scale: muscle → fascicle → muscle fibre → myofibril → actin/myosin

layers.detail: Skeletal (voluntary, striped), cardiac (heart, striped, automatic), smooth (organs/vessels, automatic).
A long muscle cell packed with myofibrils.
Repeating units (sarcomeres) of the proteins actin and myosin.
Myosin pulls on actin (powered by ATP and triggered by calcium), shortening the fibre.

entries.function: Generates movement, pumps blood, and moves contents through organs.
entries.clinical: Loss of blood supply kills muscle (heart attack); breakdown releases contents (rhabdomyolysis); nerve/calcium problems cause weakness or cramps.
entries.source: HIVE Doctor original micro-anatomy reference (standard public-domain histology, re-expressed)

entries.scale: nervous system → nerve → neuron + glia → synapse

layers.detail: The signalling cell: dendrites receive, the cell body processes, the axon sends signals.
A fatty insulating sheath on many axons that speeds signals.
The gap where one neuron passes a chemical message (neurotransmitter) to the next.
Support cells that feed, insulate, and protect neurons.

entries.function: Carries fast electrical/chemical signals for sensation, movement, and thought.
entries.clinical: Losing myelin slows signals (as in MS); blocked blood supply kills neurons (stroke); neurons mostly don't regrow, so damage can be lasting.
entries.source: HIVE Doctor original micro-anatomy reference (standard public-domain histology, re-expressed)

entries.scale: aorta → artery → ARTERIOLE → CAPILLARY → venule → vein

layers.detail: Thick, muscular, elastic vessels carrying blood away from the heart at high pressure.
The smallest arteries — their muscular walls tighten or relax to control blood flow and blood pressure.
One-cell-thick vessels where oxygen, nutrients, and waste are exchanged with tissues.
Collect blood and return it to the heart at low pressure; veins have valves to stop backflow.
Most vessels have three coats: intima (inner endothelium), media (muscle/elastic), adventitia (outer support).
The single-cell inner lining of every vessel — controls clotting, tone, and leakiness.

entries.function: Delivers oxygen/nutrients to every cell and removes waste; arterioles set blood pressure, capillaries do the exchange.
entries.clinical: Arteriole tone drives blood pressure; capillary leak causes swelling; endothelial damage starts atherosclerosis and clots; a blocked vessel starves the tissue beyond it.
entries.source: HIVE Doctor original micro-anatomy reference (standard public-domain histology, re-expressed)

entries.scale: blood → plasma + cells → red cells / white cells / platelets

layers.detail: The fluid (mostly water) carrying proteins, salts, nutrients, and waste.
Carry oxygen on haemoglobin; made in the bone marrow.
The immune defenders (several types) that fight infection.
Cell fragments that plug leaks and start clotting.

entries.function: Transports oxygen, nutrients, hormones, heat, and immune cells; clots to stop bleeding.
entries.clinical: Low red cells = anaemia; abnormal white cells = leukaemia/infection; too few platelets = easy bleeding; too much clotting = DVT/stroke.
entries.source: HIVE Doctor original micro-anatomy reference (standard public-domain histology, re-expressed)

entries.scale: heart → chambers → myocardium → cardiac muscle cells

layers.detail: Four-chambered pump with valves and its own coronary blood supply.
Endocardium (inner lining), myocardium (the thick muscle), epicardium/pericardium (outer covering).
Heart-muscle tissue that contracts as one coordinated unit.
Cardiomyocytes — branching, striped cells joined by 'intercalated discs' that pass the electrical signal cell-to-cell; packed with mitochondria.

entries.function: Coordinated contraction of cardiomyocytes pumps blood around the body.
entries.clinical: A blocked coronary artery starves a patch of myocardium and the cells die — a heart attack. Scarred or stretched muscle causes heart failure and arrhythmias.
entries.source: HIVE Doctor original micro-anatomy reference (standard public-domain histology, re-expressed)

entries.scale: lungs → lobes → bronchioles → alveoli → alveolar cells

layers.detail: Trachea → bronchi → bronchioles branch like a tree.
~300 million tiny air sacs wrapped in capillaries — the exchange surface.
Ultra-thin cells across which oxygen and CO₂ diffuse.
Make surfactant, a soap-like film that keeps the sacs from collapsing.

entries.function: Oxygen crosses the thin alveolar wall into capillary blood; CO₂ crosses out to be breathed away.
entries.clinical: Fluid or pus in the alveoli (pneumonia, heart failure) blocks exchange; too little surfactant collapses sacs; destroyed walls = emphysema/COPD.
entries.source: HIVE Doctor original micro-anatomy reference (standard public-domain histology, re-expressed)

entries.scale: kidney → cortex/medulla → nephron → glomerulus + tubule cells

layers.detail: Filters blood into urine; ~1 million filtering units each.
The working unit: a filter (glomerulus) plus a long tubule.
A tuft of capillaries that filters fluid out of the blood.
Line the tubule and reclaim water, salts, and nutrients while passing waste on as urine.

entries.function: Filters waste and balances water, salts, acid, and blood pressure, drop by drop.
entries.clinical: Damaged glomeruli leak protein/blood; lost nephrons = chronic kidney disease; a blocked, infected kidney is an emergency.
entries.source: HIVE Doctor original micro-anatomy reference (standard public-domain histology, re-expressed)

entries.topic: Gut wall — sliced to the cell
entries.scale: gut tube → wall layers → mucosa → lining cells

layers.detail: From inside out: mucosa (lining), submucosa, muscularis (the moving muscle), serosa (outer).
Finger-like folds of mucosa that hugely increase the absorbing surface.
Absorbing cells on the villi that take up digested nutrients.
Mucus-making goblet cells, hormone cells, and immune cells guarding the gut.

entries.function: Muscle layers push food along while the mucosa digests and absorbs it.
entries.clinical: Flattened villi = malabsorption (coeliac); inflamed mucosa = IBD; a full-thickness break = perforation (an emergency); mucosal cells can turn cancerous.
entries.source: HIVE Doctor original micro-anatomy reference (standard public-domain histology, re-expressed)

entries.scale: skin → epidermis → dermis → subcutis → skin cells

layers.detail: Thin outer barrier of stacked keratinocytes, renewing from the bottom up.
Pigment cells that give skin colour and protect against UV.
Tough collagen layer holding nerves, vessels, glands, and hair roots.
Fat layer for insulation and cushioning.

entries.function: A self-renewing waterproof barrier that senses, protects, and regulates temperature.
entries.clinical: Barrier loss = eczema/infection; melanocytes can turn into melanoma; deep burns destroy all layers and need specialist care.
entries.source: HIVE Doctor original micro-anatomy reference (standard public-domain histology, re-expressed)

layers.detail: Hard cortical shell over spongy inner bone, with marrow inside.
Rings of mineralised bone around a central vessel — the repeating unit.
Osteoblasts build bone, osteoclasts break it down, osteocytes maintain it — constantly remodelling.
Makes blood cells and stores fat.

entries.function: Living, remodelling tissue that supports the body, stores calcium, and makes blood.
entries.clinical: When breakdown outpaces building, bone thins (osteoporosis) and fractures easily; marrow problems affect blood cells.
entries.source: HIVE Doctor original micro-anatomy reference (standard public-domain histology, re-expressed)

entries.topic: Skeletal muscle — sliced to the cell

layers.detail: Bundles (fascicles) of muscle fibres wrapped in connective tissue, attached by tendons.
A single long muscle cell with many nuclei.
Chains of sarcomeres — the contracting units.
Overlapping actin and myosin filaments that slide to shorten the muscle.

entries.function: Converts chemical energy into pulling force to move the skeleton.
entries.clinical: Tears, overuse (tendinitis), breakdown (rhabdomyolysis), and nerve or calcium problems all show as weakness, pain, or cramps.
entries.source: HIVE Doctor original micro-anatomy reference (standard public-domain histology, re-expressed)

entries.scale: nerve → neuron → axon → synapse → next cell

layers.detail: The neuron holds a charge difference across its membrane, ready to fire.
A trigger flips the charge and a wave races down the axon.
Insulated gaps let the signal 'jump' and travel faster.
At the end, neurotransmitters cross the gap to excite or calm the next cell.

entries.function: Fast, precise signalling underlies every sensation, movement, and thought.
entries.clinical: Nerve compression, demyelination, or chemical imbalance disrupt signals — numbness, weakness, pain, seizures, or mood changes.
entries.source: HIVE Doctor original micro-anatomy reference (standard public-domain histology, re-expressed)

layers.detail: A secretory organ wrapped in a thin capsule, divided into lobules fed by blood vessels and drained by ducts (exocrine) or straight into the blood (endocrine).
Clusters of secretory cells arranged around tiny spaces or follicles where the product (hormone, enzyme, or fluid) is made and stored.
Epithelial cells packed with rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi that build and package the secretion; endocrine cells release it into nearby capillaries, exocrine cells into a duct.
The hormone or enzyme itself (a protein or steroid) — the chemical message or tool the gland exists to make.

entries.function: Glands manufacture and release the body's chemical signals and fluids — hormones that set metabolism, growth and reproduction, or enzymes and fluids for digestion and protection.
entries.clinical: Glands can under- or over-produce (e.g. thyroid, pancreas/insulin), become inflamed, form nodules or cysts, or rarely turn cancerous — which is why lumps, or changes in energy, weight or hormones, are worth checking.
